content: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) is a leading cause of maternal mortality and morbidity globally. Active management of the third stage of labour has been shown to effectively prevent PPH. While Syntometrine is more effective than oxytocin in this regard, it is associated with a higher incidence of side effects. Carbetocin, a long-acting oxytocin agonist, has emerged as a potentially effective agent for PPH prevention. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether carbetocin is as effective as conventional uterotonic agents in preventing PPH. Additionally, the review aimed to determine the optimal routes of administration and dosing for carbetocin. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to March 1, 2011. They also reviewed references from relevant articles and contacted authors and pharmaceutical industry representatives. Randomised controlled trials comparing carbetocin with other uterotonic agents, placebo, or no treatment were included in the analysis. A total of 11 studies involving 2635 women were included in the review. Six trials compared carbetocin with oxytocin. Of these, four trials focused on women undergoing caesarean deliveries, one on women following vaginal deliveries, and one did not specify the mode of delivery. In these trials, carbetocin was administered intravenously at a dose of 100 µg, while oxytocin was given intravenously at varying doses. Four trials compared intramuscular carbetocin with intramuscular Syntometrine in women undergoing vaginal deliveries. Three of these trials involved women without risk factors for PPH, while one included women with risk factors. One trial compared intravenous carbetocin with placebo. Carbetocin significantly reduced the need for additional therapeutic uterotonics compared to oxytocin in women undergoing caesarean sections (risk ratio [RR] 0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.44 to 0.88; four trials, 1173 women). However, this benefit was not observed in women who had vaginal deliveries. Carbetocin was also associated with a reduced need for uterine massage compared to oxytocin, both after caesarean delivery (RR 0.54; 95% CI 0.37 to 0.79; two trials, 739 women) and vaginal delivery (RR 0.70; 95% CI 0.51 to 0.94; one trial, 160 women). There were no significant differences between carbetocin and oxytocin in terms of the risk of PPH (blood loss >500 ml) or severe PPH (blood loss >1000 ml). When compared to Syntometrine, carbetocin was associated with lower mean blood loss (mean difference [MD] -48.84 ml; 95% CI -94.82 to -2.85; four trials, 1030 women). There was no significant difference in the need for additional uterotonic agents between the two groups. However, carbetocin was associated with significantly fewer adverse effects, including nausea (RR 0.24; 95% CI 0.15 to 0.40; four trials, 1030 women) and vomiting (RR 0.21; 95% CI 0.11 to 0.39; four trials, 1030 women). Women who received carbetocin also had a significantly lower incidence of postpartum hypertension compared to those who received Syntometrine. One study, published as an abstract, investigated the cost-effectiveness of carbetocin but provided limited data. In conclusion, carbetocin significantly reduces the need for additional therapeutic uterotonics in women undergoing caesarean sections compared to oxytocin, although it does not reduce the overall incidence of PPH. For women undergoing vaginal deliveries, carbetocin is associated with less blood loss compared to Syntometrine and has significantly fewer adverse effects. Further research is required to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of carbetocin as a uterotonic agent.
